text: This lesson closes Chapter 13 with encryption, and the honest headline matches the auditing lesson: PostgreSQL handles in-transit and column-level encryption well, but it does not have built-in Transparent Data Encryption the way Oracle and SQL Server do.

PostgreSQL supports SSL/TLS for connections, configured in postgresql.conf with certificate files, and enforced in pg_hba.conf using the hostssl connection type instead of host — directly analogous to SQL Server's Force Encryption.

pgcrypto is the real extension for column-level encryption, useful when only specific sensitive fields need protecting rather than the whole database. It also provides hashing functions commonly used for password storage.

PostgreSQL core genuinely has no equivalent to Oracle or SQL Server's Transparent Data Encryption. The real, common answer is filesystem or full-disk encryption — LUKS, BitLocker, or cloud storage-level encryption underneath the data directory.

That's three tools covering what TDE covers with one integrated feature elsewhere — not a missing feature to work around, but PostgreSQL's actual answer. Next up, starting Chapter 14: pg_dump versus physical backups.
